question: A 25-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after he was involved in a motorcycle collision. He was not wearing a helmet. Physical examination shows left periorbital ecchymosis. A CT scan of the head shows a fracture of the greater wing of the left sphenoid bone with compression of the left superior orbital fissure. Physical examination of this patient is most likely to show which of the following findings?

enhanced_information: In a patient with a fracture of the greater wing of the left sphenoid bone and compression of the left superior orbital fissure, the most likely physical examination finding is an absent left corneal reflex. This is due to damage to the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (V1), which is responsible for the sensory limb of the corneal reflex. Other cranial nerves affected by the compression do not lead to the symptoms described in the other options.
analysis: The patient's injury involves a fracture of the greater wing of the sphenoid bone with compression of the left superior orbital fissure. This anatomical location is associated with the structures passing through the superior orbital fissure, which include the oculomotor nerve (CN III), trochlear nerve (CN IV), abducens nerve (CN VI), and the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V1). Compression of these nerves can lead to various neurological deficits. The oculomotor nerve (CN III) controls most of the eye movements except those controlled by CN IV (superior oblique muscle) and CN VI (lateral rectus muscle). Therefore, damage to CN III would result in impaired eye movements, except for lateral gaze (controlled by CN VI) and intorsion (controlled by CN IV). Thus, preserved lateral gaze (option 'opc') is the most likely finding in this scenario, as the lateral rectus muscle (innervated by CN VI) would remain functional while other eye movements could be compromised.
